lesson.title: Breaking Strings Apart: The split() Method
lesson.summary: The split() method turns one string into a list of smaller strings based on a separator, converting free-form text into structured, workable data.
lesson.body:
Where strip() cleans the edges of a string, split() takes it apart entirely, turning one string into a list of smaller strings based on a separator. Calling text.split() with no arguments splits on any run of whitespace, meaning spaces, tabs, and newlines, and it also discards empty strings that would otherwise result from multiple consecutive spaces. This makes .split() the natural tool whenever you have a sentence or a line of space-separated data and you want to work with the individual pieces rather than the whole blob of text.

Trace through "the quick brown fox".split(). Python scans the string looking for whitespace boundaries: it finds "the", then a space, then "quick", then a space, then "brown", then a space, then "fox". The result is the list ["the", "quick", "brown", "fox"], four separate string elements you can now index, loop over, or count with len(). This connects directly to what String Methods already taught you about strings behaving as sequences, except now you are converting that sequence of characters into a sequence of words.

split() also accepts an explicit separator argument, which changes its behavior in an important way: it splits on exactly that separator, without collapsing repeats. Consider comma-separated data: "apple,banana,,cherry".split(",") produces ["apple", "banana", "", "cherry"]. Notice the empty string between "banana" and "cherry", because there were two commas in a row with nothing between them, and unlike the whitespace default, an explicit separator does not swallow empty results. This distinction trips people up constantly when parsing comma-separated data, so it is worth tracing by hand at least once.

A very common pattern splits a line into a fixed number of fields:

line = "Ana, 16, sophomore"
name, age, grade = line.split(", ")
print(name)   # "Ana"
print(age)    # "16"
print(grade)  # "sophomore"

Here the separator is the two-character string ", " (a comma followed by a space), so the split lands cleanly on word boundaries without leftover spaces. This is called unpacking: because split(", ") returns exactly three elements, Python can assign each one to name, age, and grade in a single line. If the line had a different number of comma-separated fields than variables on the left, Python would raise a ValueError, so this pattern only works when you know the shape of your data in advance.

There is also a maxsplit argument, text.split(",", 1), which limits the split to at most one cut, useful when you want the first field separated from everything else without breaking up commas that appear later in the remainder. For example, "key: value: extra".split(":", 1) produces ["key", " value: extra"], stopping after the first colon instead of also splitting the second one. Split is the method that turns free-form text into structured data your program can actually reason about, and it pairs naturally with the strip() method from the previous chapter, since fields pulled out by split() often need their own surrounding whitespace cleaned up afterward.
